triamcinololone modulates permeability of the ECV 304 cell line, which may have implications for age‐related maculopathy.
triamcinolole acetonide modulated the permeability of EVC304 cells in vitro, and down‐regulated expression of ICAM1, which is an adhesion molecule involved in inflammatory processes in the eye.
triamcinololone acetonidde (TA) modulates permeability, and intercellular cell‐adhesion molecule‐1 expression of the human ECV304 cell‐line.

the effects of TA on the BRB and RPE in the pathogenesis of AMD.
the modulation of cellular permeability and expression of adhesion markers, which are likely to be important in the treatment of AMD.
the development of new therapeutic strategies to combat the devastating effects of macular degeneration and other ocular diseases, such as uveitis.

TA is a potent anti‐permeability molecule and that it has the ability to reduce the expression of ICMA‐1, but not MHC‐I, in vitro.

A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
triamcinolones may be a useful treatment in AMD, but further studies are required to determine the precise mechanism of action and long term effects.

triamcinolones have been found to modulate the permeability of endothelial cells, and that this may be mediated via the down‐regulation and/or modulation of the expression of ICMA‐1.
The main takeaway from our work is that

triamcinolome acetonide can modulate the permeability of the outer blood‐retinal barrier (outer BRB) and down‐regulate the expression of intercellular adhension molecule‐1 (CAM‐1) on the ECV304 cells, suggesting that triamcinlonoe acetonide has the potential to restore the outer BRB in patients with age‐related maculopathy (AMD).
TA has the capacity to down‐regulate ICAM‐1, a molecule that is overexpressed in AMD and is thought to contribute to the pathogenesis of the disease.
TA may have a dual role in AMD, acting to reduce inflammation by decreasing the expression of ICAMS‐1 and to reduce vascular permeability, thereby reducing leakage and oedema.
